newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook-Tight supplies to prop up price.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook-Tight supplies to prop up price.

text.p: Asia's crude market should see some strength this week, as supplies from Indonesia are tighter, while Iraqi crudes remained unavailable to Japanese buyers, traders said on Monday.
Indonesia's state-owned Pertamina sharply lowered the September export allocations for the heavy sweet Widuri and Cinta crudes to a total of 21,000 barrels per day (bpd), from 83,000 bpd in August.
The September volumes of light sweet Belida crude were also cut by 60 percent to 6,000 bpd.
Only the heavy sweet Minas crude was raised to 49,000 bpd, up by 11,000 bpd from August.
The export volumes for the main Indonesian crudes in September are 157,000 bpd, from 222,000 bpd in August, traders said.
The lower crude exports are due to firmer domestic demand, as Indonesia's new 65,000-bpd crude distillation unit (CDU) at Balikpapan comes fully onstream by September, traders said.
A larger, 200,000-bpd CDU at Balikpapan also resumed operations last week after a one-month maintenance, boosting domestic demand for its crudes.
Regional demand is also likely to rise as China bought small volumes in August, and is expected to emerge in September to replenish its crude stocks, traders said.

Any respite that could come from West Africa, Asia's swing crude supplier, would be limited as only a few cargoes of West African crudes are scheduled to arrive in September and most would head to South Korea, traders said.
The closed arbitrage window between West Africa and Asia in the past two months saw only South Korean refiners buying the long-haul grades.
There was also increased buying of September loading West African crudes from China and Taiwan, but these will only arrive in October.
In addition, any hopes of Japan lifting Iraqi crudes in August were dashed following their exclusion from the first round of contracts.
Asian refiners who were postponing their September requirements on expectations of getting Iraqi crudes would now have to rely on Asian supplies, traders said.
The market started on a positive note for Middle East grades, with the first October Oman trade done on Friday at a premium of three cents to the official MPM price.
Traders had not expected October trading to start as early, and viewed the deal as a sign of a firmer market.
"The trading started earlier, and the deal was done at a premium. I see that as a positive sign," said a trader with a major oil company.
